rows.statement: In Coober Pedy, 'noodling' is searching through mullock (waste rock) heaps left by opal miners for overlooked opal, and thousands of pale cone-shaped mullock heaps cover the opal fields around the town.

rows.statement: Opal was discovered at Coober Pedy on 1 February 1915 by a prospecting party led by James Hutchison; his teenage son Willie (aged 14 or 15, sources differ) found the first piece.

rows.quote: The rock the opal sits in was laid down by an ancient inland sea. The opal itself came much later. One dating study suggests roughly twelve to sixteen million years ago, long after the sea had gone.
rows.statement: Coober Pedy opal occurs in weathered Early Cretaceous marine claystone (Bulldog Shale) deposited by an inland sea in the Eromanga Basin, but the opal formed much later: a 2015 dating study of associated alunite suggests about 12 to 16 million years ago.

rows.quote: Doors cut straight into the hillsides. Pipes poking out of the ground like snorkels.
rows.statement: Coober Pedy dugout homes have doors and facades cut into hillsides, with ventilation shafts that stick up above the ground.

rows.quote: A few metres of rock is slow to heat up and slow to cool down, so underground the temperature hardly moves. NASA puts it at about twenty-three degrees Celsius, around seventy-three Fahrenheit.
rows.statement: Because rock heats and cools slowly, Coober Pedy dugouts stay at a nearly constant temperature; NASA Earth Observatory gives about 23°C (about 73°F).

nguon.title: Keeping it Cool in the Outback

rows.quote: Residents describe roughly twenty-four all year, with no air conditioning and no heater.
rows.statement: Residents of Coober Pedy describe their dugout homes as staying around 24°C year-round without air conditioning or heating.

rows.statement: Coober Pedy has underground hotel accommodation carved into the rock.

rows.quote: According to a state heritage report, the first miners probably started digging homes within a few years of the find.
rows.statement: The first Coober Pedy opal miners probably began digging dugout homes within a few years of the 1915 opal discovery (heritage report says dugouts were likely built during the earliest mining period, 1915-1918).
